# 03 — Phishing Analysis Lab

A hands-on lab for **phishing email triage and analysis** — one of the most common daily tasks for a Tier-1 SOC analyst. Every file in this project is in English and built around a single honest principle: the training samples here are **reconstructed by me for practice**, clearly labeled as such, and no real-world incident is claimed.

Repository: https://github.com/szzxli/soc-home-lab

---

## What's in this project

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `header-analysis-cheatsheet.md` | Quick-reference: key header fields, SPF/DKIM/DMARC verdict tables, and a one-line recognition guide for common obfuscation techniques |
| `sample-walkthrough.md` | Full end-to-end analysis of a **reconstructed training sample** (labeled `RECONSTRUCTED TRAINING SAMPLE — not a real phish received`): headers → auth → multi-layer URL decoding → attachment IOCs → verdict → Tier-1 response steps |
| `gophish-selftest-guide.md` | How to send a simulated phish to **your own mailbox only** with GoPhish, then analyze it yourself using this project's method. Includes a compliance box with legal boundaries. |
| `report-template.md` | Blank phishing analysis report template (metadata / headers / auth / IOCs / verdict / actions) — ships blank by design, never pre-filled with a fabricated case |

---

## Learning path

Follow this order — each step builds on the previous one:

1. **Read the cheatsheet** (`header-analysis-cheatsheet.md`). Learn what each header field means and how to read SPF/DKIM/DMARC results at a glance. This is your desk reference for everything after.
2. **Follow the walkthrough** (`sample-walkthrough.md`). Trace a complete analysis: Received-chain reading, `Return-Path` vs `From` vs `Reply-To` mismatch, line-by-line `Authentication-Results` interpretation, multi-layer URL deobfuscation (URL-decode → Base64-decode → landing analysis), attachment IOC extraction, verdict with severity rating, and the Tier-1 response playbook.
3. **Phish yourself** (`gophish-selftest-guide.md`). Set up GoPhish, send a simulated phish to your own mailbox **only**, then analyze it with the walkthrough method *before* clicking anything. Compare your verdict against what GoPhish recorded.
4. **Write it up** (`report-template.md`). Document your self-test (or any future real report) using the template. Practice writing verdicts with evidence, severity, confidence, and recommended actions — this is what hiring managers want to see.

---

## SOC skills this maps to

Phishing triage is Tier-1 daily work. This lab demonstrates:

- **Email header analysis** — Received-chain tracing, sender-identity verification (`Return-Path` / `From` / `Reply-To`), Message-ID assessment
- **Email authentication** — reading and interpreting SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results, including alignment and domain-owner policy (`p=reject`/`quarantine`/`none`)
- **URL deobfuscation** — layered decoding (URL encoding, Base64), short-link/redirector chain expansion with `curl -I`, landing-page assessment without interaction
- **IOC extraction** — file hashing (SHA-256/MD5), embedded URL extraction from attachments, sandbox submission workflow
- **Verdict & severity rating** — evidence-weighted judgment with confidence levels and exculpatory-evidence checks
- **Incident response basics** — reporter containment, evidence preservation, blast-radius hunting, blocking, and reporting/escalation
- **Professional integrity** — reconstructed samples are labeled as reconstructed; reports are never pre-filled with fabricated cases; offensive tooling (GoPhish) is used strictly within legal and ethical bounds

These map directly to Associate Cybersecurity Analyst / SOC Analyst job descriptions: *"analyze phishing emails," "triage security alerts," "document findings," "escalate per playbook."*

---

## Honesty & compliance notes

- The walkthrough sample is **fictional and self-authored** — it says so at the top of the file. All domains are placeholders (`*.example`), all IPs are from the `192.0.2.0/24` TEST-NET-1 documentation range.
- The GoPhish guide restricts simulations to **your own mailbox**. Targeting others without written authorization may violate computer-crime laws.
- The report template is intentionally blank. A portfolio artifact built on an invented "real incident" would be a lie an interviewer could unravel in one question — this project is designed so every claim in it survives scrutiny.

---

*Part of the [soc-home-lab](https://github.com/szzxli/soc-home-lab) series — verifiable, hands-on security experience.*

# Email Header Analysis Cheatsheet

Quick-reference for Tier-1 phishing triage. Read the walkthrough (`sample-walkthrough.md`) first for the full reasoning; use this page during live analysis.

---

## 1. Key Header Fields

Read `Received` headers **bottom-up** — the lowest one is the oldest hop (closest to the original sender).

| Header | Meaning | What to look at |
|---|---|---|
| `Received` | Each mail server that handled the message, in order | Trace bottom-up; unexpected countries, free-mail relays, or IPs with no reverse DNS on the first external hop |
| `Return-Path` | Envelope sender — where bounces go; the domain SPF checks | Must be consistent with the `From` domain on legitimate mail; mismatch with `From` = forged identity until proven otherwise |
| `From` | Displayed sender (what the user sees) | Compare the domain to the real organization's domain; watch display-name spoofing (`"IT Helpdesk" <attacker@…>`) |
| `Reply-To` | Where replies actually go | If it differs from `From`, replies are diverted — common in credential phishing |
| `Message-ID` | Unique ID assigned by the sending MTA | Right-hand side should match a plausible sending host; a missing or malformed Message-ID is a (weak) anomaly |
| `Authentication-Results` | SPF/DKIM/DMARC verdicts stamped by your receiving filter | See section 2 — never trust these if *you* didn't add them (attackers can forge the header) |
| `X-Originating-IP` / `X-Sender-IP` | Client IP recorded by some providers | Useful when present, but non-standard — don't rely on it |
| `Date` | Claimed send time | Compare against the first `Received` timestamp; large skew suggests header forgery |
| `Subject` | Claimed topic | Urgency language ("expires in 24 hours", "suspended", "verify now") is a lure marker, not proof |

> **Rule of thumb:** Trust the headers your own infrastructure added (`Received` by your MX, your `Authentication-Results`). Everything above your first hop can be forged.

---

## 2. SPF / DKIM / DMARC Quick Verdicts

### SPF (does the sending IP belong to the envelope domain?)

| Result | Meaning | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `pass` | IP is authorized by the envelope domain's SPF record | Neutral-to-good; does **not** prove the `From` identity (envelope ≠ From) |
| `fail` | IP is explicitly not authorized | Suspicious — treat as forged unless a forwarding/misconfiguration explanation checks out |
| `softfail` | IP is probably not authorized (`~all`) | Weak signal; note it, keep investigating |
| `none` | Domain publishes no SPF record | No signal either way; common for small senders |

### DKIM (is the signature cryptographically valid?)

| Result | Meaning | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `pass` | Signature verifies; message unaltered since signing, tied to `d=` domain | Good — but only authenticates the `d=` domain, not the `From` address |
| `fail` | Signature present but invalid | Strong signal of tampering or forgery |
| `none` | No DKIM signature | Neutral; many legitimate senders don't sign |

### DMARC (do SPF/DKIM align with the `From` domain, per the domain owner's policy?)

| Result | Meaning | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `pass` | Either SPF or DKIM passed **and** the authenticated domain aligns with `From` | Strong positive — the `From` domain genuinely authorized this mail |
| `fail` | Neither aligned auth passed | Malicious until proven otherwise when combined with other signals |
| `none` | `From` domain publishes no DMARC record | No policy signal; fall back to SPF/DKIM + header analysis |

### Policy tags you'll see next to DMARC

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `p=none` | Domain owner asks for monitoring only — forgeries still get delivered |
| `p=quarantine` | Owner asks receivers to treat failures as suspicious (spam/junk) |
| `p=reject` | Owner asks receivers to **reject** failures outright — a `dmarc=fail` against `p=reject` is the strongest auth signal you can get |

# Phishing Analysis Report Template

> Fill in every section from the actual evidence in front of you. Do not invent details to complete a section — if a field is unknown, write `UNKNOWN` and say why. A blank or honest "unknown" is always better than a fabricated IOC.

---

## 1. Metadata

| Field | How to fill (one line each) |
|---|---|
| Report ID | `RPT-YYYY-NNN` — your own sequential numbering, e.g. `RPT-2026-014` |
| Analyst | Your name / handle |
| Date analyzed | `YYYY-MM-DD`, timezone noted |
| Source of sample | Where the email came from: user report, gateway quarantine, self-test (GoPhish), etc. **Never claim a real incident you didn't work.** |
| Sample provenance | Real user-reported phish / GoPhish self-test / reconstructed training sample (label it honestly) |
| Original `.eml` retained | Yes/No + storage location (retain for real cases; training samples may omit) |

## 2. Headers Summary

| Field | How to fill (one line each) |
|---|---|
| `From` (display + address) | Copy verbatim, e.g. `"IT Helpdesk" <it-helpdesk@corp-portal.example>` |
| `Reply-To` | Copy verbatim, or `none` |
| `Return-Path` | Copy verbatim — this is the envelope sender SPF checks |
| `Subject` | Copy verbatim |
| `Date` (header) vs first `Received` | Note any skew between claimed send time and actual receipt |
| `Received` chain (bottom-up) | List hops oldest→newest with IPs; flag the first external hop |
| `Message-ID` | Copy verbatim; note if missing/malformed |
| Sender-identity assessment | State whether envelope / From / Reply-To align or mismatch, in one sentence |

## 3. Authentication Results

Paste the `Authentication-Results` header verbatim, then fill:

| Check | Result | Interpretation (one line) |
|---|---|---|
| SPF | `pass` / `fail` / `softfail` / `none` | What was checked (envelope domain + IP) and what the result means here |
| DKIM | `pass` / `fail` / `none` | Which `d=` domain was checked; `fail` = tamper/forgery, `none` = neutral |
| DMARC | `pass` / `fail` / `none` (+ policy `p=`) | Whether auth aligned with the `From` domain; note `p=reject`/`quarantine`/`none` |
| Composite auth verdict | One line: e.g. "Triple fail against p=reject — domain owner disowns this mail" |

## 4. URLs & IOCs

One row per URL found (body links, attachment-extracted links). Decode/expand each to its final destination before listing.

| # | As displayed to user | Raw href | Decoded / expanded final destination | Registrable domain | Notes (shortener? encoding layers? lookalike?) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | _e.g. link text or button label_ | _verbatim href_ | _final landing URL_ | _e.g. evil-cdn.example_ | _e.g. Base64-in-path, 2 redirect hops_ |

**Network IOCs** (deduplicated):

| Type | Value | First seen in |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | _e.g. login.corp-portal.example_ | URL #1 landing page |
| IP | _use real observed IPs only_ | _e.g. Received hop 1_ |
| URL | _full malicious URL_ | _e.g. attachment form action_ |

**File IOCs** (if attachments present):

| Filename | SHA-256 | MD5 | Sandbox verdict | Notes |

# Phishing Email Walkthrough: Reconstructed Training Sample

> **RECONSTRUCTED TRAINING SAMPLE — not a real phish received.**
> This entire email is a fictional training artifact I built for this lab. I did not receive this email,
> I did not analyze a real phishing email from any employer, and every identifier below is fabricated.
> Hosts use `example`-style placeholder domains (per RFC 2606-style practice) and IP addresses come from
> the `192.0.2.0/24` TEST-NET-1 block (RFC 5737), which can never appear in a real delivered email.

---

## 1. Sample Provenance

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Sample ID | `SAMPLE-2026-001` (self-assigned, no external case number) |
| Source | **Authored by me** for this lab as a reconstructed training sample |
| Original raw `.eml` | Not retained — sample is illustrative, not evidentiary |
| Scenario | Credential-harvesting lure themed as a "password expires in 24 hours" IT notice |
| Status | Fictional. Never sent, never received. |

> Why reconstructed instead of a real sample? I had no access to a real corporate phishing mailbox.
> Fabricating a "I analyzed this at my last job" story would be dishonest. Building the sample myself
> still lets me demonstrate the full analysis workflow end-to-end.

---

## 2. Header Analysis

Below is the (fictional) raw header block of the sample:

```
Return-Path: <mailer-daemon@evil-cdn.example>
Delivered-To: analyst.training@example.org
Received: from mailfilter.example.net (mailfilter.example.net [192.0.2.10])
    by mx.example.org with ESMTP id 4f2a9c1d
    for <analyst.training@example.org>; Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:14:22 -0700 (PDT)
Received: from bounce.evil-cdn.example (bounce.evil-cdn.example [192.0.2.66])
    by mailfilter.example.net with ESMTP id 7b11e0aa
    for <analyst.training@example.org>; Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:13:58 -0700 (PDT)
Message-ID: <20261012091358.7b11e0aa@bounce.evil-cdn.example>
From: "IT Helpdesk" <it-helpdesk@corp-portal.example>
Reply-To: support@evil-cdn.example
To: <analyst.training@example.org>
Subject: Action required: your password expires in 24 hours
Date: Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:13:58 -0700 (PDT)
```

### 2.1 Received chain (read bottom-up — the first hop is the oldest)

| Hop | What it says | What I check |
|---|---|---|
| `bounce.evil-cdn.example [192.0.2.66]` → `mailfilter.example.net` | The message entered my fictional receiving infrastructure from a host claiming the domain `evil-cdn.example`. | Does this domain match the visible `From` domain (`corp-portal.example`)? **No.** Legitimate IT notices come from the organization's own domain, not a random "CDN" domain. Mismatch = first red flag. |
| `mailfilter.example.net [192.0.2.10]` → `mx.example.org` | Handoff between my fictional filter and mailbox servers. | In a real case I would compare these IPs against the org's MX records. Here they are placeholders for the receiving side. |
| Timestamps | Two `Received` stamps 24 seconds apart (`09:13:58` → `09:14:22`). | Consistent with a single direct hop through one filter — no weird delays or multi-country bouncing. Timing is clean; the *origin domain* is the problem, not the routing. |

### 2.2 Return-Path, From, Reply-To

- **`Return-Path: <mailer-daemon@evil-cdn.example>`** — This is the *envelope* sender (where bounces go), and it is also the domain SPF authenticates against. It belongs to `evil-cdn.example`, not `corp-portal.example`.
- **`From: "IT Helpdesk" <it-helpdesk@corp-portal.example>`** — The *display* identity the user sees. It impersonates an internal IT identity on a plausible internal domain.
- **`Reply-To: support@evil-cdn.example`** — If the recipient hits "Reply", the response goes to the attacker's domain, not the displayed sender.
